**Bug 1 — the focus is real, not a rendering glitch.** `Default`'s `play` function explicitly does `selected.focus()` → ArrowRight → ArrowLeft, ending with a swatch genuinely keyboard-focused. Storybook auto-runs `play` on every mount, so that focus ring is real DOM state left behind by the interaction test — it disappears when you click away (real focus moving), and only "returns" on hard refresh because that's what re-triggers the play function. That's a real, confirmed bug, not a design ambiguity.

Same shape of issue as the last one — nothing broken today, but a real gap worth having on record.

**What this component actually does:** `ZimmColourSwatch` renders one swatch two different ways depending on whether it gets a URL to link to:

- **Has a URL** → renders as a real link. Clicking it, or pressing Enter while it's focused, navigates — that's what makes the "no full page reload" behaviour work.
- **No URL** → renders as a plain `<span>` — think of it as an invisible box with no built-in behaviour at all, the way a `<div>` has none either.

**The problem:** both versions get labelled the same way for screen readers and keyboards — "this is a selectable option, part of a group, and it's focusable." But a `<span>` doesn't *do* anything on its own. A real `<button>` responds to Enter and Space automatically, for free, just by being a button — that's built into the browser. A `<span>` responds to nothing unless someone writes code to make it respond, and in this second branch, nobody did. So it announces itself as operable, you can Tab to it — and then nothing happens if you press Enter, press Space, or click it.

I checked what base SFCC does in the identical situation, and it renders a real `<button>` there, not a `<span>` — so base's version genuinely works, and ours, right now, in that one specific branch, doesn't.

**Why this is safe to ship as-is:** the no-URL case never actually happens on the real product page today — every real colour swatch always has a real URL to go to. That branch exists for a *future* feature — a quick-view popup, where you wouldn't want clicking a colour to navigate away from the popup. That popup doesn't exist anywhere in this codebase yet. So this broken path is currently dead code — nothing on the live site can ever reach it.

**Why flag it instead of just letting it sit:** three separate people, at three separate points in this build, independently noticed the exact same thing without any of them referencing the others. That's a strong "this is real, not a false alarm" signal, and exactly the kind of thing that's easy to silently rediscover — and be confused by — the day someone actually builds that quick-view modal and finds the swatch doesn't respond to clicks.

**The actual fix, whenever it's needed:** add an optional callback prop — something like `onSelect` — and wire it to fire on click and on both Enter and Space. Not needed today, only when a real caller with no URL shows up.

The swatch component has two ways to render, depending on whether it's given a destination URL (`href`):

That `<span>` is still labeled `role="radio"`, still gets `aria-checked`, still gets a real tab stop — meaning a screen reader announces it as "a selectable colour option," and a keyboard user can Tab to it. But there's no `onClick`, no `onKeyDown`, nothing at all wired to fire when you actually try to select it. It's a control that *announces itself as operable and isn't* — the worst kind of accessibility gap, because it doesn't fail loudly, it just does nothing when someone tries to use it.

**Why it's not a live bug today:** nothing in the real app currently calls this component without a real URL — the PDP always has one. So this exact branch of code has never actually been exercised by a real shopper.

**Why it's worth fixing before it becomes one:** the moment someone builds that quick-view modal, they'll wire the swatches into it, hit this exact branch, and ship a genuinely broken control — unless they happen to notice this gap first. Three separate people, effectively, have already stumbled onto this same thing independently: the original build, the automated code review, and my own audit. That's not a coincidence — it's a real, findable hole, just one nobody's acted on yet because nothing forces it.

i18n extraction gap: Shape B (indirect messages) silently skip; affects PR + existing code
text:
This one's the biggest of the four, and it's not really about this PR at all — this PR just happened to be the flashlight that found it.

**Background, so the mechanism makes sense:** Zimmermann ships in 8 storefronts and 11 languages. When a developer writes English text in a component, there's a tool that automatically sweeps the whole codebase looking for that text, collects it into one big file, and that file is what actually gets sent to human translators. That's "extraction" — nobody manually maintains the list of what needs translating; a script finds it for you.

**The two ways to write that text, and why only one is findable:**

```tsx
// Shape A — the tool can see this
intl.formatMessage({ id: 'zimm_colour_swatch_group.pagination.next', defaultMessage: 'Next colours' })

// Shape B — what this PR actually did, and what the tool can't see
const NEXT_PAGE_MESSAGE = { id: 'zimm_colour_swatch_group.pagination.next', defaultMessage: 'Next colours' };
intl.formatMessage(NEXT_PAGE_MESSAGE)
```

Those two produce the *identical* result when the app runs. But the extraction tool works by scanning the source code text, not by running it — it's looking for the message written out right there at the call site. In Shape B, all it sees is `intl.formatMessage(NEXT_PAGE_MESSAGE)` — a name, not the actual text — and it has no way to go find what that name points to. So it just... skips it. Silently. No error, no warning.

**What that actually means in practice:** the two new "Previous colours" / "Next colours" labels this PR added are invisible to the translation pipeline. They will never reach a translator, and they will show up in English on every one of the 11 locales, forever, unless someone catches it by hand.

**Why I called it "not new" rather than "this PR broke something":** I went and checked whether this pattern existed anywhere before this PR — and it does. `zimmProductStyleCode`, a component that's already merged and already live in production, writes its message the exact same way (Shape B), and it has the exact same problem. I confirmed it directly: zero appearances in the actual translation file. So this isn't a mistake this PR introduced — it's a mistake that's been quietly shipping for at least one prior release, and this PR's two new strings are just what led me to go check and find the pattern repeats.

**Why it's a ticket and not something to send back to Build right now:** fixing this PR's two strings alone (switching them to Shape A, or manually hand-adding them to the translation file) would patch the symptom here, but the real problem is bigger than this PR — it's a question of which way *every* Zimmermann-authored piece of text in the whole codebase should be written going forward, and whether the ones already shipped (like `zimmProductStyleCode`'s) need to be fixed too. That's a codebase-wide convention decision, not a two-line fix, and it deserves its own investigation rather than being decided as a side effect of this PR.

This one's a scope boundary, not a bug — but a real one worth understanding.

**Some background on what a "set" or "bundle" is:** sometimes Zimmermann sells multiple items together as one purchase — say, a top and a skirt sold as a "look." The product page for something like that doesn't just show one product view — it shows the *bundle* itself, plus a separate, smaller product view for *each item inside it*. So one page, several product views stacked on it.

**What this PR actually wired up:** the new, nicer colour swatches — only on the *main*, single-product view. Not on those smaller child-item views inside a bundle.

**Why that matters:** if one of those child items — the top, say — happens to come in more than one colour, that child would still show the *old*, plain circular swatches, sitting right next to the new photo-swatches on the main item, on the same page. Two different swatch styles, same page, and there'd be no clear reason to a shopper why.

**Is that happening right now?** I checked, and then asked you to check the real merchandising system directly — and you confirmed no, nothing in the actual catalogue today is a bundle or set with colour-variant children. So this is a real *capability* gap, not a live, visible bug. Nobody can actually see the inconsistency today because the situation that would trigger it doesn't exist yet.

**Why I didn't just build it anyway:** the design work for this story — the Figma file, the layout, the sizing — was only ever confirmed for the *main* product view. Nobody has designed what a colour swatch should look like squeezed into that smaller, secondary bundle-child layout. Building it anyway would mean inventing that look myself, with nobody having actually signed off on it — which isn't how this team wants design decisions made.

**Why it's a ticket rather than "hold this PR open until it's done":** it genuinely needs someone with design authority to answer "should this even look different in that smaller context, or the same?" *before* any code gets written — that's not a call this ticket, or I, can make. And there's no live product needing it yet, so there's nothing urgent forcing that design conversation to happen right now either.

Two of them, `plp.md` and `pdp.md`, both contain a line that says, roughly, *"don't build colour swatches yet — how Business Manager maps a colour to its actual swatch image still needs to be worked out."*

**The contradiction I hit:** the real Jira ticket for this work had five fully worked-out acceptance criteria, no caveat at all — just "build this." So the doc said "not yet," and the ticket said "here's exactly what to build." Those can't both be right.

**Why I didn't just pick one:** the project's own rule is that when a live instruction contradicts what's supposed to be the source of truth, I stop and ask rather than silently choosing — because either the doc is out of date, or the ticket got created without checking the doc, and only a human actually knows which. **Why I can't just make that edit myself:** there's a hard rule that the automated build tools are never allowed to write to anything under `.docs/prd/` — that's deliberately a human-only boundary, so requirements docs only ever change as someone's own considered decision, never as a side effect of a code ticket getting built. **Strip the semantics** — delete `role="radio"`, `aria-checked`, `tabIndex` from that branch:
```tsx
<chakra.span __css={styles.swatch} aria-label={name} data-testid="colour-swatch">
```
Looks *identical* on screen — this is all accessibility-tree stuff, invisible visually. A screen reader stops calling it a selectable option (because right now, it isn't one). A keyboard user tabbing through the page skips right past it. It becomes honestly inert until someone builds a real caller.

**Add the callback** — a new `onSelect?: () => void` prop, wired to both click and Enter/Space:
```tsx
<chakra.span role="radio" aria-checked={isSelected} tabIndex={isFocusable ? 0 : -1}
  onClick={onSelect}
  onKeyDown={(e) => { if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') onSelect?.(); }}
  ...>
```
Keeps announcing itself as a selectable option, keeps taking Tab stops — but now clicking or pressing Enter/Space actually *does* something, calling whatever function the caller passes in.

**The catch with option 2, and it's the whole reason I hesitated:** nothing in this codebase would actually pass `onSelect` in today — there's still no caller. So it becomes a genuinely working control with nobody yet using it. It's not wrong, exactly, but it's effort spent on a feature that doesn't exist yet, on the strength of a guess about what that future feature will need.

That's the actual tradeoff: option 1 makes today's behavior *honest* about doing nothing; option 2 makes it *capable* of something nobody's built yet.

So this is a reasoned estimate from well-established figures, not a measurement — flagging that distinction clearly rather than presenting false precision.

**Per image:**
- A full-resolution fashion product photo served unscaled (what our build requests) is typically 150–500KB — SFCC master images are usually sourced at 1500–2000px+ for zoom/gallery use, at moderate-to-high JPEG quality.
- A 96px-wide DIS thumbnail at `q=60` (what `sizedSwatchUrl` requests) is typically 2–6KB — a small JPEG at that resolution and quality is reliably in that range.
- That's roughly a **30×–100× difference per image**, not a marginal one.

**Per page load:** both builds window pagination to a maximum of 4 rendered swatches at a time (`PAGE_SIZE = 4` in both), so a multi-colour PDP mounts up to 4 of these images on load, not the full colour count.

- Unsized (ours): ~4 × 300KB (mid-estimate) ≈ **~1.2MB** of avoidable image payload
- Sized (theirs): ~4 × 4KB ≈ **~16KB**

So the realistic gap is on the order of **several hundred KB to over a megabyte** of unnecessary data per PDP visit for any multi-colour product — on mobile, against a page that `AGENTS.md` explicitly calls out as having "mobile page speed" as "a top priority" and an LCP budget of ≤2s at p75.

**One caveat on LCP specifically:** the swatches themselves are very unlikely to *be* the LCP element (that's normally the main product image), so this may not show up as a direct LCP-metric regression. But it's still real, unnecessary page weight competing for mobile bandwidth and connection slots, and it's a plain violation of the written rule regardless of whether it happens to move the LCP number.

**To get an exact number cheaply:** open a real multi-colour PDP with DevTools Network open and check the swatch image request sizes directly — that'll give you the real figure for this catalogue's actual photography in under a minute, with your own already-authenticated session.

**Practical meaning:** these 10 tests never touch the colour-swatch feature at all. They never open a browser page, never click anything, never check anything. They die instantly on a missing helper function. This isn't "the feature is broken" — it's "the test was never actually finished."

generateRegistry.mjs fix analysis: safe, tested, one latent edge case (template literals) not live today
text:
Here's the full story on that one.

**Why it exists at all:** Jhoan's new `ColourSwatches` component has a prop type with a multi-line signature — something like a callback prop whose type spans several lines (matching the pattern PreBuild flagged elsewhere: `validateOrderability?: (variant, product, quantity, stockLevel) => boolean | undefined;` split across multiple lines for readability). The repo's registry generator (`scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`) auto-scans every component's prop types to build `.claude/registry/components.md` — it runs automatically after every commit. Its existing prop-extraction logic used a single-line regex, so a multi-line type broke it: it would either mangle the entry or silently drop part of the signature.

**What the fix actually does:** she added a `normaliseBody()` function that walks the raw text of a prop block character by character, tracking parenthesis depth, and collapses any multi-line property type into one line before the regex ever sees it — so `foo?: (\n  a,\n  b,\n) => void;` becomes `foo?: (a, b,) => void;` first, then the existing regex extracts it correctly. To do that depth-tracking safely, it also has to recognize when it's *inside* a string or a comment, so a stray `(` typed inside a string literal or a `//` comment doesn't throw off the count.

**How thoroughly it was checked:** I didn't just read this and trust it — I built a copy of the old (broken) version, ran both the old and new version against every single `.ts`/`.tsx` file in `overrides/app/` (101 files, 30 of them with a `Props` type), and diffed the output. Exactly one file changed — the one this fix was written for — and it changed correctly (the old version silently dropped a parameter; the new one keeps it). Every other file produced byte-identical output. That's about as strong a "this doesn't break anything" signal as you can get without a live CI run.

**The latent gap:** the depth-tracker recognizes single quotes, double quotes, and comments as places where a stray `(` shouldn't count — but it doesn't recognize template literals (backtick strings). I proved this with a synthetic test case: a prop type containing a backtick string with an unbalanced `(` inside it (e.g. `` testId?: `prefix-(${string}` ``) causes the *next* prop in the same block to be silently dropped from the registry entry, because the fake unbalanced paren throws the depth count off.

**Why none of that matters right now:** none of the 101 real files in this codebase today have a prop type containing a backtick string — I checked. So this bug exists in the code but has zero live victims. It's a "somebody, someday, writes a prop type with a template literal in it" landmine, not a current defect.

**Why it's informational, not a PR comment:** it's not something Jhoan did wrong in a way she should fix in *this* PR — the fix she wrote is a correct, necessary, well-tested response to a real problem her component exposed. The backtick gap is a small blind spot in the fix's own scope, in shared tooling that affects the whole repo going forward, not just her feature. It's worth someone picking up as a tiny follow-up someday, but it's not blocking, not caused by negligence, and not really "hers" to own past this PR.

Here's the plain version.

**What this tool does:** `generateRegistry.mjs` is a script that automatically reads every component in the codebase and writes a summary of it — "this component takes these props, here's what each one does" — into a reference file. Nobody writes that summary by hand; the script scans the actual code and generates it.

**What broke:** Jhoan's new colour-swatch work touches `product-view/index.tsx`, which has a prop whose type definition is long enough that it spans several lines instead of fitting on one. The script's old method for reading prop types assumed everything would be on a single line — so when it hit this multi-line one, it got confused and mangled the output, actually *losing* part of the type definition entirely without any warning.

**What she fixed:** she added a small step that "flattens" a multi-line prop type back into one line before the script tries to read it — like un-wrapping a sentence that got split across multiple lines so you can read it as one sentence again.

**Why I'm calling it "safe, legitimate":** I didn't just take her word for it — I ran the tool's old version and her new version side by side against *every single component file in the whole codebase* (101 files). Only the one file her fix was meant to fix changed at all, and it went from broken to correct. Every other file produced byte-for-byte identical output. So the fix does exactly what it's supposed to and nothing else.

**Why "one latent edge case, not live today":** while testing it, I found one specific pattern her fix doesn't handle — if a prop type contains a piece of text wrapped in backticks (`` `like this` ``) that itself has an unmatched open-parenthesis inside it, the flattening logic gets confused in a *different* way and can silently delete an unrelated, neighboring prop from the documentation. I proved this with a made-up test case. But — and this is the point — I checked, and **no real file in the codebase today actually has that specific shape**. So it's a real crack in the fix, but nothing is falling through it right now.

**Why it's informational, not a PR comment:** the fix works, it's safe, and it solves a real problem correctly. The leftover gap is a "this could theoretically bite someone later" observation about shared tooling, not something wrong with what she shipped. Flagging it to Jhoan now would be asking her to fix a bug that doesn't exist yet, in a file the PR only touched incidentally — worth a note for whoever owns this script next, not a blocker on this PR.

text:
Good catch, and this one's on me. I read this exact code during the design-fidelity pass and even reasoned through part of it, but never surfaced it as a finding. Let me lay out what's actually happening.

**The code, `colourSwatches.css.ts`:**

```js
'&:focus': { zIndex: 1 },
'&:focus::after': {
  content: '""',
  position: 'absolute',
  inset: '-2px -2px calc(-1 * var(--zimm-focus-ring-offset-secondary)) -2px',
  border: 'var(--zimm-border-width-default) solid var(--zimm-color-border-focus)',
  pointerEvents: 'none',
},
```

With a comment right above it: *"`&:focus` not `&:focus-visible`: arrow-key programmatic focus doesn't reliably trigger `:focus-visible`."*

**Is this intentional?** Yes, in the sense that it's a deliberate, documented choice, not an oversight. But the reasoning behind it only holds up for half of what it's applied to.

**You're right that focus rings are meant for keyboard users specifically.** That's exactly what `:focus-visible` exists for: it's a browser heuristic that shows the ring when focus came from a keyboard, and suppresses it when focus came from a mouse click, since a sighted mouse user can already see what they clicked and doesn't need the extra visual cue. `:focus` doesn't make that distinction at all. It fires on any focus, mouse or keyboard. That's why you're seeing the ring appear on a plain click and disappear on clicking elsewhere: that's just what `:focus` does. It isn't broken exactly, but it defeats the entire point of using `:focus-visible` in the first place, and it's visual noise for every mouse user now.

**Here's the part that makes the stated justification only half right.** There are two separate places `.focus()` gets called in this component:

1. **Same-page arrow key navigation** — the swatch's `.focus()` is called synchronously, right inside the keydown handler itself. This is the standard, well-supported pattern for keyboard-driven composite widgets, and modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) reliably treat this as keyboard-visible. `:focus-visible` would work fine here.
2. **Cross-page arrow key navigation** (when arrowing past the edge of the current page) — the `.focus()` call happens inside a `useEffect`, which fires on a later render, disconnected from the original keydown event. This is the case where `:focus-visible`'s heuristic genuinely can lose track of "this came from a keyboard," since it's no longer happening within the same synchronous event.

So the comment's justification is true for case 2, but not for case 1, and case 1 is the more common path (any time someone arrows within a visible page of swatches, which is most of the time). Rather than fixing the narrow cross-page case specifically, the whole component was switched to plain `:focus`, which fixes the rare case by breaking the correct behavior for the common one.
